after: ## Why there is a need for interpretation
alt: Judges need to interpret statutes because of broad terms (Brock v DPP), ambiguity, drafting errors, new developments (R (Quintavalle)) and changes in language. Every question involves a tension between parliamentary supremacy and producing a sensible, just result.
caption: General words meet specific facts: judges balance Parliament’s supremacy against a just result.

after: ## Why there is a need for interpretation
alt: The four approaches on a line from the words to the purpose: the literal rule gives the plain meaning even if absurd (Whiteley v Chappell); the golden rule starts literally but departs to avoid absurdity (R v Allen; Re Sigsworth); the mischief rule from Heydon’s Case looks at the defect the Act cures (Smith v Hughes); the purposive approach looks at the purpose of the whole Act (Jones v Tower Boot).
caption: Each approach sits further from the bare words and closer to Parliament’s purpose.

alt: The literal rule gives words their plain meaning even if absurd (Lord Esher, 1892). In Whiteley v Chappell a man who voted as a dead person was not guilty; in Fisher v Bell a knife in a shop window was not "offered for sale"; in LNER v Berriman oiling points was not "relaying or repairing". It respects supremacy and certainty but can produce absurd results and assumes perfect drafting.
caption: Certain and respectful of Parliament, but capable of absurd results.

alt: The golden rule from Grey v Pearson starts with the literal meaning but departs from it to avoid absurdity. The narrow approach chooses between meanings: "marry" in R v Allen and "in the vicinity of" in Adler v George. The broad approach overrides a single repugnant meaning: in Re Sigsworth a murderer could not inherit from his victim. It corrects literal absurdities but has no test of absurdity.
caption: Literal first; the narrow approach picks a meaning, the broad one avoids a repugnant result.

alt: Heydon’s Case sets four questions: the common law before the Act, the mischief, Parliament’s remedy and the reason for it. In Smith v Hughes the mischief was soliciting people in the street, so prostitutes tapping on windows from balconies were guilty. Elliott v Grey and Royal College of Nursing v DHSS also applied the rule. Weaknesses: it suited short statutes, may need extrinsic aids and risks judicial law-making.
caption: Find the defect the Act was passed to cure, then read the words to suppress it.

alt: The purposive approach reads the words to achieve the purpose of the whole Act. In Jones v Tower Boot "in the course of employment" was read broadly, and in R (Quintavalle) cloned embryos were covered. In Magor and St Mellons Lord Denning said judges should "fill in the gaps"; Lord Simonds called this "a naked usurpation of the legislative function". It gives just results but is less predictable.
caption: Purpose over wording: just results, at the cost of predictability and judicial restraint.

after: ## Worked example: applying all four rules
alt: Under a fictional Act banning vehicles from a public park, the literal rule makes both Ruth’s bicycle and an ambulance offences, which is absurd for the ambulance. The golden rule avoids that by not reading "vehicle" to cover emergency vehicles. The mischief rule may catch the bicycle if the mischief is danger and noise, but not a life-saving ambulance. The purposive approach probably catches Ruth while the ambulance advances the purpose of safety.
caption: Same words, different rules, different outcomes.
